newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - Wheat price lures North African imports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Wheat price lures North African imports.

text.p: Cash-strapped North African grain importers are returning to the world market to buy wheat, taking advantage of a sharp fall in prices caused by harvesting in the United States, European grain traders said on Thursday.
But the action by Algeria, Tunisia and others has put a floor under prices and could push them higher again if buying intensifies.
"The world market may have bottomed out. There are buyers. This should support prices a bit," one French exporter said.
July Chicago futures dipped on Monday to a three-year low of $3.28 per bushel as the harvest made swift progress helped by hot dry weather in the U.S. plains.

Prices, which had crumbled from a record $7.50 a bushel in 1996, surged to $4.59 in April on concerns over frost in the United States and drought in Europe. But rain in May in Europe and reports the U.S. crop had recovered from frost have pushed world prices down.
Even so, most buyers had stayed off the market with the notable exception of Egypt and Pakistan, both major importers.
Drought-hit North-African importers, faced with sharply lower crops this year, checked prices and did nothing. But in the past week they decided it was time to move.
"They are probably getting enough reports that wheat prices now have less of a chance to drop further," one exporter said.
In early U.S. trade on Thursday wheat prices were several cents off the week's lows at $3.34 a bushel.
In a series of swoops, Algeria has bought up to 425,000 tonnes of wheat from Canada, the United States and elsewhere.
Tunisia told sellers on Thursday it was in the market for 150,000 tonnes of wheat to be shipped over the summer.
Private Moroccan operators have also been buying a few cargoes of wheat although more sustained purchases are not expected until mid-July.
Traders said it could be just the beginning. "We know North Africa will be a very good wheat buyer this year," one said.
The London-based International Grains Council said last month dry conditions would sharply cut wheat production in Morocco, Tunisia and Algeria and increase their purchases.

The IGC expects Morocco to raise wheat imports to 2.2 million tonnes in 1997/98 (July/June) from 1.4 million the previous season. Tunisia may double imports to 1.2 million and Algeria boost purchases by 800,000 tones to four million tonnes.
Egypt, an active wheat buyer last month, can afford to wait before tapping world markets again, although lower prices may prove a strong incentive.
"Egypt can wait a little bit. But it may be back within two weeks," one exporter said.

North Africa has been a traditional destination for European Union wheat, mostly French, but importers have been buying from elsewhere since April when the EU halted exports to dampen domestic prices ahead of the new harvest.
The EU passed up the opportunity to renew exports at its weekly grain meeting on Thursday, saying it had not made a decision to renew subsidies needed to assist exports.
But exporters said the world's third largest exporter after the United States and Canada could soon be forced to line up sales from what could be another huge harvest this year.
